newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish markets keep nerve after French vote.
newsitem.headline: Spanish markets keep nerve after French vote.

text.p: Spanish financial markets kept their nerve on Monday morning even though some analysts considered the French election result the worst possible for Europe's single currency prospects.
Bonos were trading around 30 basis points lower, while the peseta was weaker but bouncing back from initial dips.
"This was the worst possible result. The Socialist party won, but they will need the backing of others to rule," said Luca Jellinek, bond strategist at Paribas in London.
"That was the only outcome which could raise problems for EMU...and a delay could cause Spain problems given we have such a low spread (versus Bunds)," Jellinek added.
The Spanish 10-year spread over Bunds was trading at around 80 basis points at 0810 GMT on Monday, versus 75 at the close on Friday. It hit a record low at 64 bps on May 21.
After the Bonn-Bundesbank standoff over the German government's gold revaluation proposal, dealers in Spain said the EMU project's credibility was worse off.
"We'll either have a soft euro or no euro at all," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

The peseta reacted nervously on Monday morning, hitting a record low at 84.91 per mark, before recovering. Dealers said it was a knee-jerk reaction to the French franc slipping against the mark, but they ruled out a sharper weakening short run. At 0855 GMT it was trading at 84.70/74 per mark versus Friday's closing 84.64/67.
